analysis.one_liner: Requires Medicare drug plans to admit any qualifying pharmacy that meets standard contract terms.
analysis.headline: The bipartisan bill, with 9 cosponsors split between both parties, never received a committee vote or floor action before the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would change Medicare's prescription drug benefit so that plans and the pharmacy benefit managers that build their networks cannot exclude a pharmacy that agrees to the plan's standard contract terms. Pharmacy benefit managers, or PBMs, are middlemen hired by insurers to run drug benefits, and they often steer patients toward pharmacies they own or favor. The bill directs Medicare officials to set standards ensuring network contract terms are reasonable, which would make it harder to push locally owned pharmacies out of Medicare drug networks.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries, especially those in rural or underserved areas who depend on a nearby independent pharmacy, gain the right to fill prescriptions at any pharmacy willing to accept the plan's standard terms. Independent and community pharmacies gain access to Medicare drug networks they are often excluded from, protecting their patient base and revenue.

how_it_helps.text: Requires Medicare drug plan sponsors and PBMs to let any pharmacy that meets the plan's standard contract terms participate as a network pharmacy, ending the common practice of excluding pharmacies without cause.

Directs the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services to set standards for 'reasonable and relevant' network contract terms by January 1, 2026, so plans cannot impose predatory terms as a backdoor way of excluding pharmacies.

The bill's stated purpose is to 'assure pharmacy access and choice for Medicare beneficiaries,' preserving patients' ability to use a trusted local pharmacy rather than a PBM's preferred mail-order or specialty pharmacy.

analysis.who_pays: Pharmacy benefit managers and the insurers that own them bear the cost: they lose control over which pharmacies serve Medicare drug plans and the revenue from steering patients into their own affiliated pharmacies. Plan costs could edge up slightly if networks include higher-cost pharmacies, though the bill lets plans keep standard terms and reasonable contract conditions.
analysis.who_pays_short: Pharmacy benefit managers and their insurer owners

drawbacks.text: Any-willing-pharmacy rules can raise drug plan costs, since plans must include pharmacies with higher dispensing costs than preferred mail-order channels, and some of that cost can flow back to beneficiaries through premiums.

Federal standards for 'reasonable and relevant' contract terms would put the government in the middle of private contract negotiations between plans and pharmacies, expanding federal control over Medicare drug plan operations.
The bill addresses only Medicare drug plans, leaving commercial insurance and Medicaid networks untouched, so PBM steering practices would continue for most Americans under 65.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real and targeted: patients keep access to neighborhood pharmacies, which matters most for rural beneficiaries and people managing multiple medications. The costs are modest and mostly borne by PBMs and insurers through reduced network control and thinner margins on steering. The bill is narrow — it does not reform PBMs across the whole market — but as a Medicare-specific protection it is well designed and low risk.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the House Energy and Commerce Health Subcommittee for the rest of the Congress and was never taken up by the full committee or brought to the floor.

narrative.text: Rep. Buddy Carter, a Republican pharmacist, introduced the bill on September 12, 2023, with bipartisan original cosponsors including Rep. Debbie Dingell, a Democrat.
The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and the Ways and Means Committee on the day it was introduced.
It was referred to the Energy and Commerce Health Subcommittee on September 15, 2023, and referred there again on December 17, 2024, as the Congress wound down.
The bill never received a committee markup, a floor vote, or Senate action before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Pharmacy benefit managers and the insurers that own them came out ahead: they keep their power to decide which pharmacies serve Medicare drug plans, and local pharmacies remain excluded when PBM contract terms shut them out.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor was a Republican and 5 of 9 cosponsors were Democrats, giving the bill a roughly even bipartisan split before it stalled in committee.

industries.note: PBMs build Medicare drug networks and routinely steer patients toward pharmacies they own or favor, earning fees and margins along the way. The bill strips their power to exclude pharmacies that meet standard contract terms, hitting both their control and their revenue.
Local pharmacies gain a guaranteed path into Medicare drug networks when they accept standard terms, protecting patients who rely on them and the pharmacies' survival.
Plan sponsors lose control over network composition, which can raise administrative burden and costs, but their PBMs are also the direct target of the bill's restrictions on network design.
